title: Introducing Anyscale KubeRay Connect: Doubling down on Kubernetes | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale launched KubeRay Connect (private preview), which lets teams keep their existing KubeRay/Kueue/Argo CD/Kyverno Kubernetes stack while layering Anyscale observability, scheduling, and lifecycle management on top via admission-time CR mutation and sidecars — an explicit reversal of the old migrate-to-Anyscale-YAML requirement, packaged as a three-tier land-and-expand product (Observe, Orchestrate, Optimize).

themes.theme: Strategic pivot: meet the KubeRay ecosystem, don't replace it

insights.claim: Anyscale is removing its biggest adoption barrier for Kubernetes-native AI teams: KubeRay Connect lets customers keep KubeRay, Kueue/KAI, Argo CD, and Kyverno unchanged while adding Anyscale's observability and orchestration on top, instead of forcing a migration to Anyscale's own operator and YAML.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Signals Anyscale is prioritizing distribution over lock-in — watch whether frictionless onboarding converts the large installed base of open-source Ray-on-K8s users into paying platform customers.
insights.quote: It removes that tradeoff: keep the KubeRay stack you already run, and get Anyscale's observability and orchestration on top of it.
insights.locator: Today we are introducing Anyscale KubeRay Connect

insights.claim: Anyscale admits its prior architecture was a sales blocker: the Anyscale Operator managed Pods directly and did not understand KubeRay CRDs, so adopting the platform meant rewriting job specs, GitOps repos, and surrounding tooling.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: A vendor publicly conceding migration cost killed deals is a tell that in AI infra, compatibility with the Kubernetes-native stack — not feature superiority — is the gating factor for platform adoption.
insights.quote: moving onto the platform meant rewriting your job specs, your GitOps repos, and the tooling wrapped around them
insights.locator: Until now, adopting the Anyscale Platform

insights.claim: By building on KubeRay CRDs and leaving reconciliation to the KubeRay Operator, Anyscale inherits compatibility with the whole body of Kubernetes-native tooling (Kueue, Argo CD, Kyverno) for free, because that tooling integrates at the CRD/controller layer.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: The CRD/controller interface is becoming the de facto standard integration point for AI infra — vendors who fight it (proprietary pod management) pay an ecosystem tax; vendors who adopt it compound with every new K8s tool.

insights.claim: Anyscale structured KubeRay Connect as a deliberate land-and-expand funnel of three tiers shipped in order — Observe (telemetry, private preview), Orchestrate (cross-cluster scheduling, private preview), Optimize (price-performance tuning, coming soon) — with Observe explicitly designed as the lowest-friction entry point.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Classic observability-first wedge: telemetry data collected in Observe becomes the moat that powers Orchestrate's scheduling and Optimize's tuning — expansion revenue depends on Observe attach rates.
insights.quote: Observe is the entry point, and deliberately the lowest-friction one.

insights.claim: Anyscale's Orchestrate tier will place workloads across clusters using availability and health signals collected by the Observe tier, meaning the scheduling product is directly fed by the observability product rather than being independent.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Utilization-maximizing scheduling across GPU clusters is where the money is as GPU fleets fragment across clouds — the observability layer is the data acquisition strategy for it.

themes.theme: Architecture: admission-time mutation and control/telemetry split

insights.claim: Instead of creating Pods, Anyscale now mutates existing KubeRay specs at admission via a MutatingWebhook, injecting lightweight dataplane sidecars for observability — three components in the customer dataplane: the Anyscale Connector, an OpenTelemetry-Collector-based Cluster Telemetry Gateway, and an Observability API.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Sidecar-injection-at-admission is a minimally invasive integration pattern that lets a SaaS vendor attach to workloads it doesn't own — a template other AI infra vendors will likely copy.

insights.claim: Anyscale deliberately split the control path (Connector, needed only at pod admission) from the telemetry path (Gateway), so either can fail without taking down the other, and claims this split also yields security (identity separation) and independent autoscaling.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Fault-isolated control/telemetry separation is table stakes for selling into enterprise platform teams — it addresses the 'what happens when your SaaS goes down' objection preemptively.
insights.quote: the Connector is only needed at the beginning of a pod's lifecycle, to mutate the spec; after that it can crash without affecting any metrics already flowing
insights.locator: Splitting control from telemetry is a deliberate

insights.claim: The KubeRay Connect security model is egress-only (Anyscale's control plane never needs ingress into the customer cluster) and uses Kubernetes-native OIDC service-account tokens verified against the cluster's own JWKS instead of an Anyscale API key, with API keys only as fallback for private clusters.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Egress-only plus keyless OIDC auth is aimed squarely at security-review-heavy enterprise buyers — reduces procurement friction versus SaaS platforms that require inbound access or long-lived API keys.
insights.quote: Every connection is initiated from your dataplane. The Anyscale control plane needs no ingress into your cluster, ever.
insights.locator: Four properties come out of this design

insights.claim: Anyscale chose a fail-closed default for its mutating webhook — if the Connector is down, new KubeRay CRs are rejected rather than admitted without telemetry — explicitly preferring blocked submissions over silently incomplete workloads (behavior is configurable).
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Fail-closed is the aggressive choice for an observability add-on (many vendors fail-open to stay invisible); it reveals Anyscale positioning telemetry as a required part of the workload, not an optional layer.
insights.quote: We chose this over fail-open to avoid silently admitting workloads in an incomplete state.
insights.locator: The mutating webhook is fail-closed by default

insights.claim: The Connector is a 'thin shim' that pulls control logic from Anyscale's control plane at runtime rather than baking it into the Helm chart, so Anyscale can ship fixes without customers running Helm upgrades; Ray workloads also keep running through Anyscale control-plane outages, though job phase transitions stop updating in the console until the Connector recovers.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Server-side logic delivery shortens the vendor's iteration loop on customer infrastructure — good for velocity, but a supply-chain/control surface enterprises will scrutinize.

insights.claim: Anyscale's Telescope now correlates signals from GPU hardware (DCGM) through Kubernetes infrastructure events up to Ray applications in one view, so a slow training job and the failing GPU underneath it appear in the same place — offered on KubeRay workloads 'in minutes'.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Hardware-to-application correlation is the differentiated part of AI observability (generic APM vendors stop at the container) — a direct competitive angle against Datadog-style tools for GPU fleets.
insights.quote: a slow training job and the failing GPU underneath it show up in the same place
insights.locator: That last one is worth highlighting

insights.claim: Day-one KubeRay Connect observability includes Ray Data/Ray Train/Cluster dashboards that persist after the cluster terminates, Loki-aggregated logs, and workload/service/job events including autoscaler logs, and it works identically whether workloads are submitted via kubectl apply or the Anyscale API.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Post-mortem persistence of dashboards after cluster teardown targets a known open-source Ray pain point — a concrete value hook for converting OSS users.
insights.locator: What you get on day one

insights.claim: Anyscale's next steps after the private preview are multi-cluster orchestration (the Orchestrate tier using Observe's health/availability signals), identity passthrough mapping cluster identity to platform identity for RBAC/attribution/quotas, and multi-region serving for services.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Multi-cluster, multi-region GPU workload placement is the emerging battleground among AI compute platforms — Anyscale is racing to own the scheduling layer above increasingly fragmented GPU capacity.

insights.claim: The 'doubling down on Kubernetes' framing implies Anyscale has concluded that the Kubernetes-native open-source stack for Ray is too entrenched to displace, so its commercial value must come from observability intelligence and scheduling layered above it, not from owning the runtime.
insights.speaker: Elizabeth Hu
insights.so_what: Read-through for AI infra investing: the orchestration/runtime layer is commoditizing to open source; durable margins migrate to telemetry, placement, and cost-optimization layers on top.
insights.locator: Introducing Anyscale KubeRay Connect: Doubling down
